mainTopic: The powers and limits of an אפוטרופוס caring for orphans, and the rule that orphans' property is like הקדש in sales.
overview: The משנה teaches that a person caring for orphans, whether a homeowner they live with or an אפוטרופוס their father appointed, must tithe their produce. It also brings a dispute about which kind of אפוטרופוס swears when he hands the property back. The גמרא asks how a steward can tithe produce that is not his, and רב חסדא answers that he may tithe food the orphans will eat now but not produce being stored. A long ברייתא then lists a steward's limits. He may spend on מצוה items with a fixed cost but not on open-ended ones. He may not go to court in a way that risks a loss, make risky land trades, or free the orphans' slaves. Stories follow: רבי מאיר stops a steward from trading land for slaves and ignores a dream, he makes peace between two people who always fought, and רבי יהושע בן לוי allows trading land for plowing oxen. רב נחמן rules that an old woman the orphans lived with could sell their ox. He also teaches שמואל's rule that orphans' property, like הקדש, is acquired only with money. The גמרא works out how this rule applies when prices rise or fall. רב שישא insists it must never be used in a way that hurts the orphans, and his last objection continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A caretaker of orphans must tithe their produce
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a homeowner who looks after orphans, or an אפוטרופוס appointed by their father, must separate מעשרות from the orphans' produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNA: Orphans who rely on a homeowner, or whose father appointed a steward for them: he is obligated to tithe their produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens with a rule: the person taking care of orphans has to tithe their produce for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two kinds of caretakers are listed. One is a homeowner the orphans simply live with, even without a formal appointment. The other is an אפוטרופוס officially appointed by their father. Both have the duty, and the power, to separate מעשר from produce that belongs to the orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה'. It marks the start of the משנה text.
A homeowner, here someone the orphans live with who handles their affairs
A steward or guardian who manages someone else's property
To tithe, meaning to separate מעשרות from produce

steps.confusionAlert: The produce here belongs to the orphans, not to the caretaker. That is exactly why the גמרא will soon ask how he is allowed to tithe it.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Orphans who relied
phrases.notes: Literally 'leaned on': the orphans live with this person and he takes care of them.

phrases.english: on a homeowner,
or whose father appointed a steward for them,
he is obligated to tithe their produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ יְתוֹמִין שֶׁסָּמְכוּ אֵצֶל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A homeowner caring for orphans, or an אפוטרופוס appointed by their father, must tithe the orphans' produce.

steps.title: Which steward must take an oath: a dispute
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא says an אפוטרופוס appointed by the father takes a שבועה and one appointed by בית דין does not. אבא שאול says it is the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: A steward appointed by the orphans' father takes an oath. If the court appointed him, he does not take an oath. אבא שאול says: the matters are reversed.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second rule about stewards: when he returns the property, must he swear he took nothing for himself? Two opinions disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the first opinion, only the father's appointee swears; the court's appointee is exempt. אבא שאול flips this completely: the court's appointee swears and the father's appointee does not. The משנה states the dispute without giving reasons.

keyTerms.meaning: The matters are reversed: the opposite of what was just said

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה has two separate rules: (1) a caretaker must tithe orphans' produce; (2) a dispute over whether the father's appointee or the court's appointee takes a שבועה.

phrases.english: A steward who was appointed
by the orphans' father takes an oath.
phrases.notes: The oath is taken when he hands the property back, swearing he took nothing of theirs for himself.

phrases.english: If the court appointed him, he does not take an oath.
Abba Shaul says: The matters are reversed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate rule in the same משנה about stewards of orphans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא: the father's appointee swears and the court's appointee does not. אבא שאול: the reverse.

steps.title: A ברייתא says a steward cannot separate תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contrasts the משנה with a ברייתא that reads the word 'אתם' (you) to exclude partners, sharecroppers, stewards, and anyone separating תרומה from produce that is not his.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא raises a contradiction: 'You' – but not partners; 'you' – but not sharecroppers; 'you' – but not stewards, and not one who separates תרומה from what is not his!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first rule of the משנה by quoting a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the word 'אתם' in the פסוק that only the owner can separate תרומה. It specifically lists אפוטרופין as people who cannot. Yet our משנה said an אפוטרופוס must tithe the orphans' produce, so the two sources seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא; marks the start of the discussion on the משנה
'And contrast them': the גמרא sets two sources against each other
Sharecroppers who work a field for a share of the crop

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question about whether orphans' produce needs tithing; it does. The question is whether someone who is not the owner has the power to do it.

phrases.english: GEMARA: And they raised a contradiction:
"You" – but not partners;
phrases.notes: The word is from במדבר 18:28, about giving תרומה.

phrases.english: "You" – but not sharecroppers;
"You" – but not stewards,
and not one who separates teruma from what is not his!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first rule of the משנה (step 1), that a steward tithes the orphans' produce.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that an אפוטרופוס must tithe the orphans' produce.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא derives from 'אתם' that only an owner may separate תרומה and explicitly excludes אפוטרופין, so how can the משנה require a steward to tithe?

steps.title: Tithing to feed versus tithing to store
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers that the משנה deals with produce the steward tithes so the orphans can eat it, while the ברייתא deals with produce he wants to store away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: It is not difficult. Here it is to feed them; there it is to put it aside.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא resolves the contradiction by saying each source is talking about a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה allows the steward to tithe produce the orphans need to eat, since he cannot feed them untithed food. The ברייתא forbids him to tithe produce that is just being put aside, because he is not the owner and has no authority there. So the general rule of 'אתם' stands, with an exception for the orphans' food.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer
It is not difficult; the two sources do not really conflict
To feed: produce given to the orphans to eat
To put aside: produce stored, not eaten now

steps.whatToRemember: A steward may tithe orphans' produce only for what they will eat (להאכיל). He may not tithe produce that is just being stored (להניח), because it is not his.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the basic rule that only an owner can separate תרומה stays in place, and the steward's power is a limited exception based on the orphans' needs.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said: It is not difficult:
Here it is to feed; there it is to put aside.
phrases.notes: The first 'here' is our משנה and the second 'there' is the ברייתא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source refers to a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed the משנה and ברייתא conflict over whether a steward can tithe the orphans' produce.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה permits tithing produce the orphans will eat. The ברייתא forbids tithing produce that is merely stored.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the feeding-versus-storing distinction
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says stewards separate תרומה and מעשרות, and sell the orphans' property, only to feed them now and not to store away for later.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in a ברייתא: Stewards separate תרומה and מעשרות to feed the orphans, not to store the produce. They may sell animals, slaves, houses, fields and vineyards to feed the orphans, but not to save the money. They may sell produce, wine, oil and flour to feed them, but not to save the money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that says exactly what רב חסדא said: tithing is allowed to feed the orphans, but not to store the produce away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא resolved the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא by splitting the cases into eating now versus storing. This ברייתא spells out that same split, so his answer now has a source. The ברייתא also applies the same rule to selling the orphans' property: selling is allowed to buy them food now, not to build up savings.

keyTerms.meaning: And indeed it is taught in a ברייתא (used here to bring support)
To feed, so that the orphans can eat now
To put aside, meaning to store away for later

phrases.english: And it is taught: The stewards separate terumah and tithes
to feed, and not to put aside.
phrases.notes: This is רב חסדא's split from step 4: produce they will eat now, versus produce stored away.

phrases.english: And they sell for them cattle, male and female slaves,
houses, fields and vineyards –
to feed, but not to put aside.

phrases.aramaic: וּמוֹכְרִין לָהֶן פֵּירוֹת, יֵינוֹת, שְׁמָנִים וּסְלָתוֹת –
phrases.english: And they sell for them produce, wines, oils and fine flour –
to feed, but not to put aside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that supports רב חסדא's answer in step 4.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's distinction between tithing so the orphans can eat now and tithing to store produce away.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא (תוספתא תרומות 1:10) that says stewards tithe 'to feed, and not to put aside'.

steps.title: Stewards may buy מצוה items that have a fixed cost
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: stewards may make or buy מצוה items with a set cost for the orphans. The גמרא adds that שופר and מגילה are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: Stewards make for the orphans a לולב, a ערבה, a סוכה, ציצית, and anything with a fixed cost. This includes a שופר. They buy for them a ספר תורה, תפילין, מזוזות, and anything with a fixed cost. This includes a מגילה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps listing the steward's powers. Now it says he may spend the orphans' money on מצוה items with a set price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key test is קצבה, a fixed and limited amount. A לולב or a ספר תורה costs a known sum, so the orphans' money is not at risk of endless spending. The גמרא adds short comments ('לאיתויי') to show which extra items the phrase 'anything with a fixed cost' brings in.

keyTerms.meaning: A fixed, limited amount or cost
To include; the גמרא is showing what an extra phrase adds
The willow branch used on סוכות

steps.confusionAlert: The 'לאיתויי' lines are not part of the ברייתא. They are the גמרא's own short comments explaining what the phrase 'anything with a fixed cost' adds.

phrases.english: And they make for them a lulav and a willow branch
and a sukkah and tzitzit,
and anything that has a fixed amount;
to include a shofar.
phrases.notes: This is the גמרא talking now, telling us what 'anything with a fixed amount' adds.

phrases.english: And they buy for them a Torah scroll,
tefillin and mezuzot,
and anything that has a fixed amount;
to include a Megillah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a new category: מצוה spending.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A steward may spend the orphans' money on מצוה items with a fixed cost, including a שופר and a מגילה.

steps.title: No open-ended spending from the orphans' money
steps.stepSummary: Stewards may not pledge צדקה, free captives, or pay for anything without a fixed cost, such as comforting mourners, from the orphans' money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Stewards do not pledge צדקה on the orphans' behalf, and do not free captives on their behalf, nor do anything that has no fixed amount. This includes comforting mourners.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives the other side of the rule: spending with no fixed limit is not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Things like צדקה and פדיון שבויים have no ceiling, so they could drain the orphans' money. That is why they are not allowed, even though they are great מצוות. The גמרא again adds that comforting mourners falls into this group.

keyTerms.meaning: Pledging a set amount of charity

steps.whatToRemember: The dividing line is קצבה: fixed-cost מצוות are allowed from the orphans' money, while open-ended ones are not.

phrases.english: And they do not pledge charity on their behalf,
and they do not redeem captives on their behalf,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ קִצְבָה;
phrases.english: nor anything that has no fixed amount;
to include comforting mourners.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite side of step 6: open-ended spending is not allowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A steward may not commit the orphans' money to spending with no fixed limit, such as צדקה, freeing captives, or comforting mourners.

steps.title: Stewards may not go to court for the orphans
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says stewards may not take part in court cases about the orphans' property, whether to lose or to gain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Stewards are not allowed to go to court, either to take on a loss or to gain, regarding the orphans' property.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds one last rule: stewards may not go to court over the orphans' property. This sets up the גמרא's question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Banning a loss makes sense. But the ברייתא also seems to ban going to court to gain, which sounds strange, since winning only helps the orphans. That oddness is what the גמרא challenges next.

keyTerms.meaning: To go to court and argue a case
To take on a loss or an obligation

phrases.english: And stewards are not permitted to go to court –
to lose or to gain –
regarding the property of orphans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Last clause of the same ברייתא, on a new topic: going to court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stewards may not take part in court cases over the orphans' property, as the ברייתא first states it.

steps.title: Why not go to court to gain?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a steward would be stopped from going to court when it can only bring the orphans gain.
steps.simpleTranslation: To gain — why not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא. If going to court helps the orphans, why should it be forbidden?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A steward is there to protect the orphans' interests. Stopping him from winning something for them makes no sense, so the wording 'or to gain' cannot be meant simply.

phrases.english: To gain – why not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the litigation clause in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'לחוב ולזכות', which seems to ban even litigation that brings gain.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Litigation that only benefits the orphans should obviously be allowed, so banning it makes no sense.

steps.title: The ban is on taking a loss in order to gain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the ברייתא as banning litigation where the steward takes on a loss now in the hope of a gain later.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read it as: 'to take on a loss in order to gain' regarding the orphans' property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the phrase differently. It is not two separate cases (lose, or gain). It is one case: taking a loss in order to gain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pure gain is allowed. What is forbidden is a gamble, where the steward puts the orphans' property at risk now and hopes it pays off later. This fits the theme of the whole ברייתא: protect the orphans' property and avoid risky or open-ended commitments.

keyTerms.meaning: In order to; on condition that
Rather; the גמרא is correcting how to read the text

steps.whatToRemember: A steward may act for the orphans' clear benefit. He may not risk their property, whether through open-ended spending or a court case that starts with a loss.

phrases.english: Rather, 'to lose in order to gain'
regarding the property of orphans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 9 by reinterpreting the ברייתא's wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא bans both losing and gaining as two separate cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא bans only litigation that takes on a loss in the hope of a later gain.

steps.title: No selling a far or poor field to buy back a near or good one
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that an אפוטרופוס may not sell the orphans' distant field to buy back a nearby one, or a poor field to buy back a good one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Stewards may not sell a far-away field to buy back a nearby one, or a bad field to buy back a good one.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds another limit on the אפוטרופוס: no trading one of the orphans' fields for a field their father once sold, even when the trade looks like an improvement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a nearby or better field seems like a smart upgrade. Even so, the ברייתא forbids the swap. The גמרא will explain why in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: To redeem, meaning to buy back a field the father had sold

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a sale for cash. The steward would be swapping one field the orphans own for a field their father had sold. The swap looks like a gain, and it is still forbidden.

phrases.english: And stewards are not permitted to sell [a field] that is far away
and redeem [one] that is nearby;
phrases.notes: "Redeem" means buying back a field that the orphans' father had sold.

phrases.english: [or to sell] a bad [field] and redeem a good one.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין אַפּוֹטְרוֹפִּין רַשָּׁאִין לִמְכּוֹר בְּרָחוֹק וְלִגְאוֹל בְּקָרוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list in the ברייתא of things a steward may not do.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A steward may not sell a far or poor field to buy back a near or good one.

steps.title: The reason: the new field might be ruined
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the swap is forbidden and answers that the field he buys back might be struck by blight.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Because perhaps [the fields] will become blighted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a swap that looks like an upgrade is forbidden, and it gives the reason right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new field could be hit by blight. Then the steward would have traded away a sound field for a ruined one and caused the orphans a loss. This fits the earlier rule from step 10: a steward should not take risks with the orphans' property in the hope of a gain.

keyTerms.meaning: They become blighted (crops struck by disease or scorching wind)

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Because perhaps they will become blighted.
phrases.notes: "They" means the fields he would buy back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the ruling in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is a seemingly favorable field swap forbidden?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The new field might become blighted, which would cause the orphans a loss.

steps.title: Trading fields and slaves
steps.stepSummary: A steward may not sell fields to buy slaves. The תנא קמא lets him sell slaves to buy fields, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל forbids even that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Stewards may not sell fields to buy slaves, but they may sell slaves and buy fields with the money. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: they may not even sell slaves to buy fields.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a new rule about trading the orphans' fields and slaves, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with part of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees he may not turn fields into slaves, because land is the more stable asset. The first opinion allows turning slaves into land because it seems safer. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל forbids even that, and the גמרא will explain why next.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the first opinion here

phrases.english: And stewards are not permitted to sell fields
and buy slaves,
but they may sell slaves
and buy fields with them.
phrases.notes: "With them" means with the money from selling the slaves.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף לֹא לִמְכּוֹר עֲבָדִים וְלִיקַּח שָׂדוֹת.
phrases.english: Not even to sell slaves and buy fields.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין אַפּוֹטְרוֹפִּין רַשָּׁאִין לִמְכּוֹר שָׂדוֹת וְלִיקַּח עֲבָדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next rule in the ברייתא's list of a steward's limits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling fields to buy slaves is forbidden. Selling slaves to buy fields is allowed by the תנא קמא and forbidden by רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.title: Why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל forbids buying fields
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the fields bought might not be secure, because others could claim them.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Perhaps [the fields] will not be secure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל forbids selling slaves to buy fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land usually seems safe, but a newly bought field might face ownership claims from others. Then the steward would have dragged the orphans into trouble. So רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that he should leave things as they are.

keyTerms.meaning: Are smooth or secure, meaning free of outside claims

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Perhaps they will not be secure.
phrases.notes: Literally "not smooth." Someone else might claim the fields.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view in step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why may a steward not even sell slaves to buy fields?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fields might not be secure from outside claims.

steps.title: A steward may not free the orphans' slaves
steps.stepSummary: An אפוטרופוס may not free the orphans' slaves, but he may sell them to others, and those buyers may free them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Stewards may not set slaves free. But they may sell them to others, and the others may set them free.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds that a steward cannot set the orphans' slaves free himself, but he has a way around it: selling them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Freeing a slave gives away the orphans' asset for nothing, so it is forbidden. Selling the slave at full price is a fair business deal. Once the buyer owns the slave, he may free him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין אַפּוֹטְרוֹפִּין רַשָּׁאִין לְהוֹצִיא עֲבָדִים לְחֵירוּת;
phrases.english: And stewards are not permitted to set slaves free;
but they may sell them to others,
and the others set them free.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין אַפּוֹטְרוֹפִּין רַשָּׁאִין לְהוֹצִיא עֲבָדִים לְחֵירוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next rule in the ברייתא, still about the orphans' slaves.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A steward may not free the orphans' slaves but may sell them to others who free them.

steps.title: רבי: the slave may buy himself free
steps.stepSummary: רבי adds that the slave himself may pay his own value to the steward and go free, since that is like selling him to himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי says: I say that even he, the slave, may pay his own value and go free, because it is as if the steward sold him to himself.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי stretches the rule from step 15: the buyer can be the slave himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban is only on giving the slave away for free. If the slave pays his full value, the orphans lose nothing. It works just like a sale to an outsider.

keyTerms.meaning: As if he sold him to him(self)

phrases.english: Rabbi says: I say,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הוּא – נוֹתֵן דְּמֵי עַצְמוֹ וְיוֹצֵא,
phrases.english: even he gives his own value and goes free,
because it is as if [the steward] sold him to him[self];

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אוֹמֵר: אוֹמֵר אֲנִי, אַף הוּא נוֹתֵן דְּמֵי עַצְמוֹ וְיוֹצֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the rule in step 15 to a sale to the slave himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slave may pay his own value to the steward and go free, since that counts as a sale.

steps.title: Does the steward give a final accounting?
steps.stepSummary: The first opinion says the steward must settle accounts with the orphans at the end. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says he does not have to.
steps.simpleTranslation: He must calculate with them at the end. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: he does not have to.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a dispute about whether the אפוטרופוס must go over all the income and expenses with the orphans when he hands the property to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion requires a full accounting of everything he spent and earned. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל exempts him, since the steward is trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: To calculate, to give an accounting
At the end (when the orphans grow up)

phrases.english: And he must calculate with them at the end.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ.
phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: He is not required.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from specific deals to the steward's duty when his job ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא requires a final accounting with the orphans. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל does not.

steps.title: Who may be appointed as steward
steps.stepSummary: The court does not appoint women, slaves or minors as stewards, but if the orphans' father appointed one of them, it stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not appoint women, slaves or minors as stewards. But if the orphans' father appointed them, he has the right to do so.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by listing who the court does not appoint as an אפוטרופוס, and it gives an exception when the father makes the choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court itself will not pick women, slaves or minors for this job. A father may choose anyone he trusts for his own children, and his choice is valid.

keyTerms.meaning: He has the right (to do so)

steps.whatToRemember: An אפוטרופוס must protect the orphans' property and avoid risky trades, even ones that look like gains. He may not give their assets away, but he may sell them at full value. The court does not appoint women, slaves or minors, though a father may.

phrases.english: We do not make as stewards
phrases.notes: "We" means the court.

phrases.english: women, slaves or minors,
but if the father of the orphans appointed them,
he has the right [to do so].

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין עוֹשִׂין אַפּוֹטְרוֹפִּין נָשִׁים וַעֲבָדִים וּקְטַנִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the ברייתא's list with who may serve as steward.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court does not appoint women, slaves or minors as stewards, but a father's appointment of them is valid.

steps.title: רבי מאיר stops a steward from selling land to buy slaves
steps.stepSummary: A steward near רבי מאיר was selling the orphans' land and buying slaves, and רבי מאיר did not let him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A steward who lived near רבי מאיר was selling the orphans' land and using the money to buy slaves. רבי מאיר did not allow it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a steward who swapped the orphans' land for slaves, and רבי מאיר stopped him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land is a lasting, safe asset, while slaves can run away or die. So trading land for slaves puts the orphans' property at risk, and רבי מאיר blocked it. The next step tells what happened after he did.

keyTerms.meaning: A steward or guardian who manages orphans' property

phrases.english: There was a certain steward
who was in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood,
who was selling lands
and buying slaves,
and Rabbi Meir did not let him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא אַפּוֹטְרוֹפּוֹס דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבָבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the rules about what a steward may do, the גמרא brings a practical story about a steward's trades.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A steward may not sell the orphans' land in order to buy slaves.

steps.title: רבי מאיר ignores a dream that seemed to disagree with him
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר was shown in a dream 'I want to destroy and you build?!', but he ignored it, saying dreams carry no weight.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a dream they showed רבי מאיר the words: 'I want to destroy, and you are building?!' Even so, he paid no attention. He said: Words of dreams do not raise up and do not bring down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר gets a dream message that seems to tell him to let the orphans lose money, but he refuses to change his ruling because of a dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dream suggested that Heaven wanted these orphans' property to fall apart, so protecting it was going against Heaven. רבי מאיר answered that dreams have no power to change a ruling of הלכה. He kept protecting the orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: They make no difference either way

steps.whatToRemember: Dreams do not decide הלכה: 'דברי חלומות לא מעלין ולא מורידין.'

phrases.english: They showed him in his dream:
"I want to destroy, and you are building?!"
phrases.notes: The message means Heaven wanted these orphans' property ruined, and רבי מאיר was protecting it.

phrases.english: Even so, he paid no attention,
he said: Words of dreams
do not raise up and do not bring down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of רבי מאיר and the steward.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dreams have no legal force. They do not change a ruling.

steps.title: רבי מאיר makes peace between two people who always fought
steps.stepSummary: Two people stirred up by the שטן fought every ערב שבת at twilight. רבי מאיר held them back for three weeks until they made peace.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two people whom the שטן stirred up, so every Friday at twilight they fought with each other. רבי מאיר came there and held them back for three Friday twilights, until he made peace between them.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the last story was about רבי מאיר, the גמרא adds another story about him: he ended a long-running fight between two people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a side story and is not about stewards. They fought at the busiest, most stressful time, just before שבת. רבי מאיר kept stopping them until there was real peace.

keyTerms.meaning: The שטן stirred them up against each other

phrases.english: There were two people
whom the Satan stirred up against each other,
so that every twilight
phrases.notes: Twilight here means Friday at dusk, right before שבת.

phrases.english: they would quarrel with each other.
Rabbi Meir happened to come there,
he held them back for three twilights,
until he made peace between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ בֵּי תְרֵי דְּאִיגָּרִי בְּהוּ שָׂטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side story brought because it is also about רבי מאיר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר worked patiently to end a fight between two people.

steps.title: The שטן complains that רבי מאיר drove him out
steps.stepSummary: After the peace, רבי מאיר heard the שטן say: Woe, רבי מאיר has driven that man out of his home.
steps.simpleTranslation: He heard the שטן saying: Woe, רבי מאיר has driven that man out of his home.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the שטן admitting defeat: once there was peace, he had nowhere to live.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that the שטן 'lives' where people fight. Making peace removes him completely.

keyTerms.meaning: That man (a polite way of saying 'me')

steps.whatToRemember: Where there is fighting, the שטן is at home. Making peace drives him out.

phrases.english: He heard him saying:
phrases.notes: The one speaking is the שטן.

phrases.english: Woe, that Rabbi Meir has driven out
that man from his home.
phrases.notes: 'That man' is the שטן talking about himself in a roundabout way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the peace-making story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fighting gives the שטן a home. Peace drives him away.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי allows a steward to sell land to buy oxen
steps.stepSummary: A steward near רבי יהושע בן לוי sold the orphans' land to buy oxen, and רבי יהושע בן לוי said nothing against it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A steward who lived near רבי יהושע בן לוי was selling land and buying oxen, and רבי יהושע בן לוי did not say anything to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to stewards. Here a steward traded land for oxen, and the חכם did not object. The next step explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This looks like the רבי מאיר case, where the steward sold land and bought something else with the money. But here the purchase was oxen, not slaves, and there was no objection. The next step explains the difference.

phrases.english: There was a certain steward

phrases.aramaic: דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבָבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי,
phrases.english: who was in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's neighborhood,
who was selling land
and buying oxen,
and he did not say anything at all to him;

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא אַפּוֹטְרוֹפּוֹס דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבָבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the steward topic with a case that seems similar to רבי מאיר's but has a different outcome.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A steward selling land to buy oxen was not stopped.

steps.title: Why: like רבי יוסי, an ox counts as part of the field
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי follows רבי יוסי, who called his ox 'my field', so buying a plowing ox is like buying land.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds like רבי יוסי, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי יוסי said, In all my days I never called my wife 'my wife' or my ox 'my ox.' Rather, I called my wife 'my home' and my ox 'my field.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי יהושע בן לוי's silence by bringing a ברייתא of רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי saw the ox that plows as the heart of the field, just as a wife is the heart of the home. So trading land for oxen is not really losing the land's value; the ox keeps the farm productive. That is why this case differs from slaves.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds like (follows the view of)
As it is taught in a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי is not just being poetic. The גמרא uses his words to show that an ox counts as part of the field, which is why the steward may buy oxen but not slaves.
steps.whatToRemember: Slaves: the steward may not trade land for them (רבי מאיר). Plowing oxen: allowed, because 'my ox' is 'my field' (רבי יוסי).

phrases.english: He holds like Rabbi Yosei —
as it is taught: Rabbi Yosei said:
In all my days I never called my wife "my wife"
or my ox "my ox",
rather, my wife I called "my home",
and my ox "my field."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רבי יהושע בן לוי's silence in the previous step.
steps.raayaObject: That a steward may sell land to buy oxen.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבי יוסי calling his ox 'my field.'

steps.title: Relatives ask why an old woman sold the orphans' ox
steps.stepSummary: Orphans lived with an old woman who sold their ox for them. Their relatives asked רב נחמן what right she had to sell it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some orphans were living with an old woman. They had an ox, and she took it and sold it for them. Relatives came before רב נחמן and said: What business does she have selling it?
steps.whatsHappening: A new case: an old woman who was never appointed steward sold the orphans' ox, and the relatives challenge her authority. This sets up רב נחמן's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 discussed who may be appointed steward. Here nobody appointed her at all, so the relatives argue she had no right to sell.

keyTerms.meaning: What business is it of hers?

phrases.english: There were some orphans
who were living with a certain old woman.
They had an ox,
she took it and sold it for them.
Relatives came before Rav Nachman,
they said to him: What business does she have selling?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new practical case about an unappointed person managing orphans' property.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a woman who cared for orphans, without being appointed, have authority to sell their property?

steps.title: רב נחמן: someone orphans live with has a steward's authority
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers from the משנה: 'orphans who lean on a homeowner', so the person caring for them acts as a steward even without an appointment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: We learned in the משנה, 'Orphans who rely on a homeowner.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the relatives by quoting a line from the משנה that covers exactly this situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats a householder whom orphans rely on as their steward, even without any formal appointment. Since the orphans lived with this old woman and she cared for them, she had that authority and her sale stands.
steps.whatToRemember: A person whom orphans actually live with and rely on has a steward's authority, even without an official appointment.

phrases.english: He said to them:
"Orphans who relied on a homeowner"
we learned.

steps.triggerLanguage: יְתוֹמִים שֶׁסָּמְכוּ אֵצֶל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the relatives' question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה gives steward status to whoever the orphans rely on, so the old woman's sale is valid.

steps.title: The relatives object: the ox went up in value
steps.stepSummary: The orphans' relatives push back against רב נחמן: the ox became more valuable, so the orphans lost out.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ox went up in value!
steps.whatsHappening: The relatives are not satisfied with רב נחמן's answer that the old woman counts as a steward. They raise a new complaint: the ox is now worth more than it was sold for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if she had the right to sell, a sale that causes the orphans a loss might be undone. The relatives argue that the rise in price shows the orphans were shortchanged.

keyTerms.meaning: it became more expensive, it went up in value

phrases.english: But it went up in value!
phrases.notes: "It" is the ox the old woman sold. The relatives are still the ones talking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new objection to רב נחמן's approval of the sale in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that the old woman's sale holds
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ox's rise in value suggests the orphans suffered a loss, so the sale should be undone.

steps.title: It rose in value after it already belonged to the buyer
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that the ox gained value only after it was in the buyer's hands, so the orphans lost nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: It went up in value while it was already in the buyer's possession.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rejects the relatives' complaint. The price went up only after the sale, when the ox already belonged to the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sale was fair at the time it happened. A later rise in price is the buyer's gain, not the orphans' loss.

keyTerms.meaning: in the possession of, in the domain of

phrases.english: It went up in value in the buyer's possession.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Timing distinction: the value rose after ownership had passed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ox's higher value means the orphans were cheated.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sale price was fair when the sale happened. The later increase belongs to the buyer.

steps.title: The relatives object: the orphans never received the money
steps.stepSummary: The relatives raise a stronger point: the buyer had not yet paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they have not yet received the money!
steps.whatsHappening: The relatives try again with a new argument. The orphans never got paid, so maybe the ox does not yet belong to the buyer at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's last answer took for granted that the ox already belonged to the buyer. If the money was never paid, that assumption may be wrong. In that case the rise in price happened while the ox still belonged to the orphans.

keyTerms.meaning: they took hold of, they received

phrases.english: But they did not receive the money!
phrases.notes: "They" means the orphans: the buyer had not paid them yet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the assumption behind the answer in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 28 that the ox was already in the buyer's possession
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No payment was made. So maybe ownership never passed, and the increase happened while the ox still belonged to the orphans.

steps.title: רב נחמן agrees: orphans' property is acquired only with money
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן admits that if no money was paid, שמואל's rule applies: orphans' property is like הקדש and is acquired only by payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: If so, this is the case of what רב חנילאי בר אידי said in the name of שמואל: orphans' property is like consecrated property, and it is acquired only with money.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן agrees with the relatives on this point. Because the orphans were never paid, the sale is not final, and the orphans can still ask for the higher price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, pulling an item (משיכה) completes a sale of movable property. שמואל teaches that orphans' property works like הקדש, where only paying the money completes the sale. So as long as the buyer has not paid, the orphans keep the upper hand.

keyTerms.meaning: property dedicated to the בית המקדש

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule of שמואל is the key idea for the rest of the passage. Every case that follows is judged by it.

phrases.english: He said to them: If so,
phrases.notes: רב נחמן is speaking to the relatives. "If so" means: if the money really was not paid.

phrases.aramaic: הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל –
phrases.english: this is the case of what Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi said in the name of Shmuel –

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: for Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi said in the name of Shmuel:
Orphans' property is like consecrated property,
and it is acquired only with money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אִם כֵּן, הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב נחמן accepts the objection of step 29 and explains it with שמואל's rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since the money was not paid, the sale is not final. Orphans' property, like הקדש, is acquired only with money.

steps.title: The case of רבנא עוקבא's wine
steps.stepSummary: Buyers pulled the orphan רבנא עוקבא's wine at four per barrel. Before they paid, the price rose to six, and the case came to רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wine of רבנא עוקבא the orphan: they pulled it at four each, and it rose in value and stood at six each. They came before רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, similar case. It sets up the question for רב נחמן to rule on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers had done משיכה, pulling the wine, which would usually finish the sale. The question is whether the orphan can still demand the higher price, since the buyers had not yet paid.

keyTerms.meaning: they pulled it (the act of משיכה that acquires movable items)

phrases.english: The wine of Rabbana Ukva the orphan –
they pulled it at four each,
phrases.notes: Four per barrel was the agreed price, and pulling the wine into their possession is what usually completes a sale.

phrases.english: and it went up in value and stood at six each.
They came before Rav Naḥman,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case that tests the rule from step 30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the orphan demand the new, higher price even though the buyers already pulled the wine?

steps.title: רב נחמן rules with שמואל's rule again
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that this is exactly the case of רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule: orphans' property is acquired only with money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: This is the case of רב חנילאי בר אידי, for רב חנילאי בר אידי said in the name of שמואל: orphans' property is like consecrated property, and it is acquired only with money.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the wine case using the same rule. Since the buyers had not paid, the sale was not final, and the higher price counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pulling the wine was not enough, because orphans' property needs payment, just like הקדש. So the buyers must pay the new price of six or let the sale fall through.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידִי –
phrases.english: He said to them: This is the case of Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi –

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידִי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: for Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi said in the name of Shmuel:
Orphans' property is like consecrated property,
and it is acquired only with money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the case in step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The pulling did not finish the sale, so the orphan gets the higher price.

steps.title: If the produce went up in value, שמואל's rule applies
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sums up: if a buyer pulled orphans' produce and its price rose before he paid, the case falls under רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone pulled produce from orphans and it went up in value, this is the case of רב חנילאי בר אידי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the general rule. It starts with the case where the price went up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the price rises, the orphans benefit from the rule that only money completes the sale. They are not stuck with the old, lower price.

phrases.english: If someone pulled produce from orphans,

phrases.aramaic: אִיַּיקּוּר – הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידִי.
phrases.english: and it went up in value – this is the case of Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the two cases into a general rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If the price rose, the sale is not final without payment, so the orphans gain the increase.

steps.title: If the produce went down in value, the buyer cannot back out
steps.stepSummary: If the price dropped, the buyer cannot use the 'only money acquires' rule to cancel. An ordinary owner should not be worse off than הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it went down in value, the power of an ordinary person should not be more limited than that of הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the rule with the opposite case, where the price dropped. Here the buyer is held to the sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With הקדש, the Temple treasury always wins whichever way the price moves. The orphans get the same treatment: the rule that 'only money acquires' helps them when prices rise. It cannot be turned against them when prices fall.

keyTerms.meaning: an ordinary person (as opposed to הקדש)

steps.whatToRemember: Orphans' property is like הקדש: the orphans always come out ahead. If the price rises before payment, the buyer must pay more. If it falls, the buyer cannot back out.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that 'acquired only with money' lets the buyer escape when prices drop. The rule exists to protect the orphans, so it only works in their favor.

phrases.english: If it went down in value –

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְהֵא כֹּחַ הֶדְיוֹט חָמוּר מֵהֶקְדֵּשׁ.
phrases.english: the power of an ordinary person should not be more limited than that of the Temple.
phrases.notes: The buyer already pulled the produce, which normally locks in a sale. The orphans' special rule can't leave them weaker than an ordinary seller, so he can't back out.

steps.triggerLanguage: זוּל – לֹא יְהֵא כֹּחַ הֶדְיוֹט חָמוּר מֵהֶקְדֵּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes step 33 with the opposite case, a falling price.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When the price falls, the pulling holds, and the buyer is bound to the sale. The orphans are never worse off than הקדש.

steps.title: Orphans pulled produce and the price went up
steps.stepSummary: Produce was pulled on behalf of the יתומים but not yet paid for. The price then rose. The יתומים keep the purchase, because an ordinary person should not be worse off than הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: If produce was pulled for the orphans and then the price went up, the rule is: an ordinary person's position should not be harsher than that of הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new case where the יתומים are the buyers. Produce was pulled for them, and then the price went up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier steps the יתומים were the sellers. Now they are the buyers, and the pulling (משיכה) already took place. Since the price rose, the deal stays in place, so the orphans get the produce at the old, lower price.

keyTerms.meaning: was pulled (the act of pulling that finalizes a purchase, משיכה)
the position of an ordinary person

phrases.english: If produce was pulled for the orphans,
and it went up in price,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְהֵא כֹּחַ הֶדְיוֹט חָמוּר מֵהֶקְדֵּשׁ.
phrases.english: the position of an ordinary person should not be harsher than that of the Temple.
phrases.notes: The same line as in step 34. Here it means the orphans keep the produce at the price from when it was pulled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Flips steps 33-34: now the orphans are buyers instead of sellers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If produce was pulled for orphans and its price rose, the orphans keep the purchase at the original price.

steps.title: Price dropped: students think the orphans can back out
steps.stepSummary: If the pulled produce dropped in price, the students thought this was a case for רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule: only money finalizes a deal with orphans, so the יתומים could cancel.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the price went down, they understood from this that it is the case of רב חנילאי בר אידי.
steps.whatsHappening: The students suggest that if the price fell, the יתומים can cancel because they have not paid yet. This is only a suggestion, and the גמרא is setting up the next step, where it gets rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students used רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule that only money acquires for orphans. Since no money was paid, the orphans could back out and buy at the new, cheaper price. The phrase 'they understood from this' signals that this view is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: it became cheaper, the price dropped
the אמורא who said orphans' property is acquired only with money

steps.confusionAlert: 'סבור מינה' (they thought) means a view that the גמרא is about to reject. It is not the final ruling.

phrases.english: If it became cheaper,
they understood from this
phrases.notes: 'They' are the students in the study hall. This phrase usually introduces an idea that will be turned down.

phrases.english: that this is the case of Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi;
phrases.notes: His rule from step 32: with orphans, only money finalizes the deal.

steps.triggerLanguage: זוּל סְבוּר מִינָּה הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Covers the opposite price movement from step 35 and proposes using רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposed: if the price dropped, the orphans may cancel since they have not paid.

steps.title: רב שישא: that rule would hurt the orphans
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי rejects the students' idea. If orphans could always cancel until they pay, no one would sell them produce until they paid in full, and sometimes they badly need food.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said to them: This is bad for them, because sometimes they need produce, and no one will give it to them until they pay the money.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא rejects the idea from step 36. He says that treating orphan buyers this way would actually hurt them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The special rules for orphans are meant to protect them, not to harm them. If sellers knew the orphans could cancel after pulling, they would demand cash first, and the orphans could go without produce they need. So for orphan buyers, pulling finalizes the deal as usual, and they cannot cancel when the price drops.

keyTerms.meaning: רב שישא, son of רב אידי
there is no one who will give

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches the idea behind all the orphan rules: they exist to help the orphans, so a rule that would harm them is not applied.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi said to them:
This is bad for them,
because sometimes they need produce,
and there will be no one who gives it to them
until they give money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי הָא רָעָה הִיא לְדִידְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the students' suggestion in step 36.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects applying רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule when orphans are buyers who pulled produce.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rule would make sellers refuse to give orphans produce without cash first, which hurts the orphans.

steps.title: Orphans paid money and the price went down
steps.stepSummary: The יתומים paid money for produce but did not pull it. The price then dropped. Money alone does not finalize an ordinary deal, so the יתומים can back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the orphans gave money for produce and it became cheaper, the position of an ordinary person should not be harsher than that of הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a second case: the יתומים paid, but the produce was never pulled. The price then went down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For ordinary people, paying money without pulling does not finalize a purchase. So the deal is not complete, and the orphans may cancel and buy at the new lower price. The seller does not get a stronger hold than הקדש would.

phrases.english: If the orphans gave money for produce,
phrases.notes: They paid, but the produce was never pulled into their hands.

phrases.english: and it became cheaper,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְהֵא כֹּחַ הֶדְיוֹט חָמוּר מִן הֶקְדֵּשׁ.
phrases.english: the position of an ordinary person should not be harsher than that of the Temple.
phrases.notes: Here it means the orphans can back out, since only paying, without pulling, does not finish a normal deal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case to step 35, but with money paid instead of produce pulled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If orphans paid but did not pull and the price dropped, they may cancel the purchase.

steps.title: Price rose after orphans paid: students think the money finalized it
steps.stepSummary: If the price rose after the יתומים paid, the students thought רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule applies: money finalizes deals with orphans, so the יתומים keep the cheap price.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the price went up, they understood from this that it is the case of רב חנילאי בר אידי.
steps.whatsHappening: The students suggest that because the orphans already paid, the deal is final, so the seller cannot back out when the price goes up. This is only a suggestion, and it sets up רב שישא's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of step 36. Here the students use רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule to help the orphans hold onto a good deal. Once again, 'they understood from this' tells us an objection is coming.

phrases.english: If it became more expensive,
they understood from this
that this is the case of Rav Ḥanilai bar Idi;
phrases.notes: The students mean that, for orphans, paying money is enough to finish the deal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיַּיקַּר סְבוּר מִינַּהּ הַיְינוּ דְּרַב חֲנִילַאי בַּר אִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Covers the opposite price movement from step 38 and again proposes using רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposed: if the price rose after the orphans paid, the money finalized their purchase.

steps.title: רב שישא begins to object again
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי starts to reject the students' second idea with the same opening words: 'This is bad for them.' His reason continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said to them: This is bad for them...
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא begins rejecting the suggestion in step 39. The גמרא is setting up his explanation, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses the exact same opening as in step 37, so we already know his approach: a rule meant to help orphans must not end up hurting them. Why this rule would hurt them is explained in the lines that follow.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi said to them:
This is bad for them,
phrases.notes: His sentence stops here. He finishes his reason on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי הָא רָעָה הִיא לְדִידְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins rejecting the students' suggestion in step 39, using the same words as step 37.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects applying רב חנילאי בר אידי's rule when orphans paid and the price rose.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rule would end up harming the orphans; the full reason continues on the next amud.
